To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) people tend to exaggerate their past performance when they are asked about their past performance, (2) people tend to overestimate their current performance when they are currently engaged in the goal that is reflected in the performance they are estimating, and (3) people tend to underreport their current performance when their current performance is not currently relevant to the goals they are currently pursuing.
people tend to exaggerate both their current performance and their past performance, but the reasons for these exaggerations are different.

(a) people exaggerate their current performance (e.g., GPA) to a greater degree than they do their past performance (e.g. SAT scores), (b) this is due to motivated self-enhancement for the former but to reconstructive memory biases for the latter, and (c) the former is more malleable and amenable to change.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why individuals exaggerate current and past performance and how this is related to motivated self-enhancement.
the question of how people come to know themselves, how their self-concepts develop, and how they come to have the sense of self that they do.
a distinction between two different types of biases in self-reports: motivated self-enhancement versus reconstructive memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the authors have provided evidence that self-reports of past and present performance are influenced by different processes and that this distinction has important implications for research on the self.

self-reports of current performance are influenced more by motivated self-enhancing concerns than are self-reports of past performances, and self-reports of performance are influenced by both motivated self-enhancing and reconstructive memory concerns.
self-enhancement is a major reason for the exaggeration of current performance but not for the exaggeration for past performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the self-enhancing bias in self-evaluation is not universal, but is rather limited to self-evaluations of currently important goals and activities.
people tend to be more accurate when reporting past performance (e.g., SAT scores) than current performance (e.g. GPA).
motivated self-enhancement is more important for self-reports of current performance than past performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self-reports are not always self-reports.
people are motivated to exaggerate their current performance because it is currently relevant and important to them.
the same person can exaggerate his or her performance for different reasons at the same time.
